passages.text: Rhythmic Metabolism in Osteosarcopenia: Emerging Evidence, a Chronometabolomic Framework for the Bone-Muscle Unit, and Research Priorities

Osteosarcopenia combines low bone mass or skeletal fragility with sarcopenia, yet its metabolic biology is commonly assessed using single-time-point measurements. <sentence_start/>We conducted a structured narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, Embase and Scopus from inception through 28 June 2026, supplemented by ScienceDirect, Google Scholar and citation chaining. <sentence_start/>Evidence was classified as direct human osteosarcopenia evidence, indirect human evidence, preclinical evidence or conceptual inference. <sentence_start/>Here, chronometabolomics denotes time-anchored or repeated metabolomic profiling used to estimate variation in phase, amplitude and pathway coordination in relation to sleep, feeding, activity and endocrine timing. <sentence_start/>Direct human evidence remains scarce. <sentence_start/>Component-specific human studies and experimental models suggest, but do not establish, that aging, chronic disease and irregular schedules may alter glucose-insulin, amino-acid, lipid, mitochondrial, redox-inflammatory, mineral-endocrine and microbial rhythms relevant to the bone-muscle unit. <sentence_start/>Chronometabolomics is therefore an emerging research framework, not a validated diagnostic or therapeutic approach. <sentence_start/>Daytime light, sleep regularization, protein distribution, time-restricted eating, exercise timing and medication timing remain candidates for controlled trials rather than current clinical recommendations; safety evaluation must address frailty, low body mass index, malnutrition, kidney disease, diabetes, polypharmacy, falls and inadequate protein or calcium intake.
1. Introduction

Osteosarcopenia describes the clinically important overlap between low bone mass or skeletal fragility and sarcopenia. <sentence_start/>It is associated with falls, fractures, disability, frailty and mortality, although current evidence does not establish that these risks exceed the additive effects of bone and muscle impairment considered separately [<citation rid="B1-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcsm.13392" pmid="38086772" pmcid="PMC10834350" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>No universally accepted case definition exists. <sentence_start/>Most studies operationalize osteosarcopenia as concurrent osteopenia or osteoporosis, usually assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) or fragility-fracture criteria, and sarcopenia diagnosed using a named consensus algorithm, such as EWGSOP2 or AWGS 2019, that incorporates low muscle strength and low muscle quantity or quality, with poor physical performance used to indicate severity [<citation rid="B2-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/ageing/afy169" pmid="30312372" pmcid="PMC6322506" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="B3-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jamda.2019.12.012" pmid="32033882" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Definitions, thresholds and DXA sites vary across cohorts and should not be treated as interchangeable.

The bone-muscle unit provides a conceptual framework for studying the combined phenotype. <sentence_start/>Endocrine signals, inflammatory mediators, nutrient handling and tissue-derived secretory factors may interact across organs [<citation rid="B4-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1530/JOE-25-0234" pmid="40899683" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B5-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3892/etm.2023.11888" pmid="37021068" pmcid="PMC10067545" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Endocrine crosstalk and RANKL-related signaling are plausible routes through which bone loss and muscle decline may reinforce one another [<citation rid="B6-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jot.2023.09.007" pmid="38021216" pmcid="PMC10654153" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B7-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1530/JOE-24-0093" pmid="38913537" count="1">7</citation>], while broader reviews place the combined phenotype within metabolic aging, multimorbidity and functional decline [<citation rid="B8-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00774-023-01472-5" pmid="38066326" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B9-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metabol.2023.155533" pmid="36907247" count="1">9</citation>].

Most explanatory models emphasize static abnormalities, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered sex-hormone exposure, glucocorticoid excess, insufficient protein intake, reduced mechanical loading and gut microbial dysbiosis. <sentence_start/>These mechanisms have empirical support to varying degrees, but their temporal organization is less well characterized. <sentence_start/>Glucocorticoid signaling illustrates the issue because local and systemic exposure may shape metabolism, muscle catabolism and bone remodeling in a phase-dependent manner [<citation rid="B10-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1530/EJE-21-0553" pmid="34478405" count="1">10</citation>,<citation rid="B11-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2026.05.002" pmid="42208534" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In chronic kidney disease, cortisol dysregulation occurs alongside altered mineral metabolism and inflammation, making an untimed measurement difficult to interpret [<citation rid="B12-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2022.1075809" pmid="36733794" pmcid="PMC9886668" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Bone turnover markers show diurnal variation [<citation rid="B13-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00223-022-00965-1" pmid="35305134" count="1">13</citation>], and the human metabolome changes across endogenous and behavioral cycles [<citation rid="B14-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/metabo11050328" pmid="34069741" pmcid="PMC8161100" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An unchanged daily mean may therefore coexist with altered amplitude, phase or exposure duration, although these features have not been validated as osteosarcopenia biomarkers.

The circadian timing system offers one organizing layer for this biology. <sentence_start/>Circadian timing has become an explicit topic in sarcopenia research [<citation rid="B15-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s41999-024-01129-0" pmid="39747789" pmcid="PMC12014836" count="1">15</citation>], and sleep-circadian interactions are increasingly studied in relation to skeletal muscle metabolic health [<citation rid="B16-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.smrv.2022.101700" pmid="36272396" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In healthy young men, experimental circadian misalignment altered the skeletal muscle lipidome [<citation rid="B17-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202100143R" pmid="33977623" pmcid="PMC12315975" count="1">17</citation>]; 24-h profiling identified different muscle metabolic patterns in older, metabolically compromised men and young healthy men [<citation rid="B18-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111786" pmid="36516749" count="1">18</citation>]; and age was associated with differences in the temporal structure of the plasma lipidome [<citation rid="B19-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s42003-023-05102-8" pmid="37474677" pmcid="PMC10359364" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In observational studies of older adults, circulating metabolites were associated with rest-activity rhythm characteristics, but these findings do not establish that behavioral rhythm disruption caused the metabolic differences [<citation rid="B20-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/sleep/zsaf320" pmid="41071097" pmcid="PMC12795739" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/sleep/zsaf319" pmid="41071109" pmcid="PMC12795748" count="1">21</citation>].

Exercise timing extends this concept from observation to intervention biology. <sentence_start/>A randomized crossover study in people with type 2 diabetes found time-of-day differences in multi-tissue metabolomic and skeletal muscle proteomic responses to exercise [<citation rid="B22-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metabol.2022.155268" pmid="35908579" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Human and experimental studies also associate resistance-exercise timing with BMAL1/PGC1 4-FNDC5/irisin signaling [<citation rid="B23-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jshs.2024.100968" pmid="39187065" pmcid="PMC11863284" count="1">23</citation>], diurnal variation in mitochondrial function and exercise capacity [<citation rid="B24-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202402930R" pmid="39902884" pmcid="PMC11792768" count="1">24</citation>], and HIF1 -mediated substrate preference [<citation rid="B25-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2504080122" pmid="40627397" pmcid="PMC12280960" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Complementary human profiling and preclinical studies implicate clock proteins in substrate metabolism and muscle performance [<citation rid="B26-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/clinem/dgae350" pmid="38779872" pmcid="PMC11913097" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP285955" pmid="38922907" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP285523" pmid="38051503" pmcid="PMC11607886" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B29-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2422446122" pmid="40324095" pmcid="PMC12088385" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="B30-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP285585" pmid="38850551" pmcid="PMC11607892" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings are not osteosarcopenia-specific and do not identify a universally beneficial exercise time.

Bone is also time-structured. <sentence_start/>Human evidence is most direct for diurnal variation in bone turnover markers and associations between rest-activity rhythms and osteoporosis-related outcomes [<citation rid="B13-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00223-022-00965-1" pmid="35305134" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="B31-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bone.2025.117521" pmid="40374023" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reviews and mechanistic studies connect clock biology with bone energy metabolism, endochondral formation, collagen hydroxylation and growth-plate biology [<citation rid="B32-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12967-021-03068-x" pmid="34579752" pmcid="PMC8477514" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2022.960456" pmid="36238690" pmcid="PMC9550872" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B34-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-021-00919-4" pmid="35094018" pmcid="PMC8991200" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B35-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-023-01152-x" pmid="37029304" pmcid="PMC10244380" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Evidence involving endothelial BMAL1, muscle <italic>Bmal1</italic>, PER1 and glucocorticoid troughs is primarily preclinical [<citation rid="B36-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI176660" pmid="39680455" pmcid="PMC11645155" count="1">36</citation>,<citation rid="B37-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/acel.70582" pmid="42259765" pmcid="PMC13246325" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="B38-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jbmr/zjag025" pmid="41641971" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B39-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/acel.70479" pmid="41952537" pmcid="PMC13062760" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Clock genes and microRNAs should therefore be viewed as research targets rather than established therapeutic targets in osteosarcopenia [<citation rid="B40-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.biopha.2022.114019" pmid="36423544" count="1">40</citation>,<citation rid="B41-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1631/jzus.B2100958" pmid="35794684" pmcid="PMC9264112" count="1">41</citation>].

We therefore examine osteosarcopenia through a hypothesis-generating framework of temporal metabolic disorganization within the bone-muscle unit (Figure 1). <sentence_start/>Here, chronometabolomics refers to time-anchored or repeated metabolomic profiling used to characterize variation in metabolite abundance and pathway behavior in relation to endogenous phase and behavioral cycles such as sleep, feeding and activity. <sentence_start/>We use circadian for endogenous approximately 24-h regulation, diurnal or time-of-day variation for patterns observed under ordinary environmental and behavioral conditions, and rest-activity rhythm for a behavioral proxy rather than a direct measure of endogenous phase. <sentence_start/>We evaluate whether aging, chronic disease and irregular behaviors may reshape the timing of amino-acid turnover, glucose utilization, lipid oxidation, mitochondrial energetics, redox balance, mineral metabolism and bone-muscle signaling. <sentence_start/>We do not treat this proposed temporal disorganization as an established mechanism of osteosarcopenia.
2. Review Design, Literature Search and Evidence Framework

This article is a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. <sentence_start/>Its conduct and reporting were informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) domains of justification, aims, search description, referencing, scientific reasoning and presentation of relevant data [<citation rid="B42-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s41073-019-0064-8" pmid="30962953" pmcid="PMC6434870" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The review was not prospectively registered. <sentence_start/>PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection (including Science Citation Index Expanded), Embase and Scopus were searched from database inception through 28 June 2026. <sentence_start/>ScienceDirect and Google Scholar were used as supplementary discovery platforms, and backward and forward citation chaining was used to locate relevant primary studies. <sentence_start/>Search concepts combined osteosarcopenia or bone-muscle phenotypes; circadian, sleep or behavioral timing; metabolomics or rhythmic metabolic pathways; tissue crosstalk; and time-targeted interventions. <sentence_start/>Appendix A reports source-specific search syntax and the role of each source.

Evidence was considered for inclusion when a peer-reviewed human observational or intervention study, repeated-sampling metabolomic or lipidomic study, or relevant experimental model addressed at least two of the following: a bone or muscle phenotype, endogenous or behavioral timing, metabolic or tissue-crosstalk pathways, and a time-targeted intervention. <sentence_start/>Reviews and consensus statements were used for context and citation discovery, with primary studies preferred for evidentiary claims. <sentence_start/>Duplicate reports, publications without a relevant bone or muscle outcome, reports without a temporal or metabolic component, and conference abstracts, editorials or isolated case reports were not used as primary evidence. <sentence_start/>No publication-date restriction was imposed; recent work from 2021-2026 was prioritized, while earlier studies were retained when required for foundational concepts.

Titles and abstracts were assessed for relevance, followed by full-text assessment of potentially informative reports. <sentence_start/>Selection was purposive and prioritized directness to osteosarcopenia, human relevance, study design, temporal resolution, methodological detail and the ability to address a defined mechanistic or translational question. <sentence_start/>The search did not produce an auditable, deduplicated record log suitable for a PRISMA flow diagram. <sentence_start/>Duplicate independent screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment and quantitative certainty grading were not performed; these features distinguish this narrative synthesis from a systematic review and are acknowledged as limitations. <sentence_start/>We did not reconstruct record counts retrospectively because doing so would imply a level of systematic-review reproducibility that the original search was not designed to provide.

Evidence was interpreted using four categories. <sentence_start/>Tier 1 denotes direct human evidence in participants with a defined osteosarcopenia phenotype and a relevant temporal measure. <sentence_start/>Tier 2 denotes indirect human evidence from sarcopenia, osteoporosis, frailty, sleep, metabolic or other informative cohorts. <sentence_start/>Tier 3 denotes preclinical or mechanistic evidence from animal, tissue or cellular models. <sentence_start/>Tier 4 denotes conceptual inference that has not been tested directly. <sentence_start/>Throughout the review, “associated with” is used for observational findings, “supports” is reserved for reproducible evidence within the studied population and design, and “may” or “hypothesized” identifies extrapolation. <sentence_start/>We identified no human study that simultaneously assessed a defined osteosarcopenia phenotype, a validated endogenous circadian phase marker and serial metabolomic profiles.

The literature is broad but uneven. <sentence_start/>Evidence is relatively more extensive for muscle metabolic timing, bone turnover-marker variation, rest-activity associations, nutrient timing and exercise timing than for their joint study in osteosarcopenia. <sentence_start/>This description reflects breadth and directness, not a formal certainty rating. <sentence_start/>Table 1 summarizes the evidence categories, osteosarcopenia-specific status and main interpretive boundaries.
3. Temporal Organization of the Bone-Muscle Unit

The suprachiasmatic nucleus coordinates physiology with the light-dark cycle, while peripheral tissues contain local clocks influenced by feeding, physical activity, endocrine exposure, body temperature and autonomic inputs. <sentence_start/>Skeletal muscle, bone, liver, intestine, kidney, immune cells and vascular endothelium can therefore exhibit tissue-specific temporal patterns. <sentence_start/>External cues may transduce timing information to peripheral molecular clocks [<citation rid="B56-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202501289R" pmid="40917013" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Whether loss of coordination among these systems contributes to osteosarcopenia remains an open question.

Skeletal muscle is a major site of glucose disposal, amino-acid turnover and fatty-acid oxidation. <sentence_start/>Experimental studies implicate the skeletal-muscle clock in insulin sensitivity, substrate handling, mitochondrial function, protein turnover and myokine secretion, although evidence for several downstream processes remains preclinical. <sentence_start/>Experimental circadian misalignment altered the muscle lipidome in healthy young men [<citation rid="B17-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202100143R" pmid="33977623" pmcid="PMC12315975" count="1">17</citation>], while 24-h profiling identified different metabolic patterns in older, metabolically compromised men and young controls [<citation rid="B18-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111786" pmid="36516749" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Exercise timing also modified metabolomic and skeletal muscle proteomic responses in type 2 diabetes [<citation rid="B22-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metabol.2022.155268" pmid="35908579" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These studies support standardizing sampling time but do not establish circadian causality in osteosarcopenia.

Bone also has substantial temporal organization. <sentence_start/>Bone turnover markers show diurnal variation in humans [<citation rid="B13-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00223-022-00965-1" pmid="35305134" count="1">13</citation>], and experimental studies connect clock biology with endochondral bone formation, collagen hydroxylation, endothelial support and inflammatory osteoclastogenesis [<citation rid="B34-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-021-00919-4" pmid="35094018" pmcid="PMC8991200" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B35-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41418-023-01152-x" pmid="37029304" pmcid="PMC10244380" count="1">35</citation>,<citation rid="B36-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI176660" pmid="39680455" pmcid="PMC11645155" count="1">36</citation>,<citation rid="B37-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/acel.70582" pmid="42259765" pmcid="PMC13246325" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A daily trough in glucocorticoid signaling appears important for skeletal health in mice [<citation rid="B39-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/acel.70479" pmid="41952537" pmcid="PMC13062760" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prospective human evidence associates rest-activity rhythms with osteoporosis risk [<citation rid="B31-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bone.2025.117521" pmid="40374023" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These observations motivate testing whether altered remodeling timing contributes to bone loss; they do not show that such disruption occurs in osteosarcopenia.

Aging and chronic disease are associated with reduced rhythm amplitude, fragmented sleep-wake cycles, lower daytime light, nocturnal light exposure, altered melatonin and cortisol profiles, irregular meals, reduced activity amplitude and polypharmacy. <sentence_start/>Under the proposed model, these factors may produce misalignment between environmental, behavioral and tissue-level timing. <sentence_start/>Late eating may shift metabolic responses relative to activity; reduced outdoor activity may weaken both light exposure and mechanical loading; and sleep fragmentation may alter endocrine or inflammatory exposure. <sentence_start/>These examples are hypotheses that require direct testing in osteosarcopenia (Figure 2).
4. Chronometabolic Pathways in Osteosarcopenia

A temporal perspective recognizes that disease-relevant metabolites can vary with endogenous phase, clock time and behavior. <sentence_start/>A pathway may differ in its mean level, within-day range, estimated phase or relationship to feeding and activity, but those features require appropriate sampling and cannot be inferred from a single measurement. <sentence_start/>Figure 3 summarizes the proposed network, and Table 2 identifies candidate readouts, evidence tiers and osteosarcopenia-specific validation status.

Glucose and insulin provide an informative example because skeletal muscle accounts for substantial postprandial glucose disposal, while bone participates in energy metabolism through osteocalcin, marrow adiposity and osteoblast energy demand. <sentence_start/>Human studies demonstrate morning-to-evening differences in metabolic state [<citation rid="B63-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jdi.13810" pmid="35429128" pmcid="PMC9434593" count="1">63</citation>], whereas causal evidence for tissue-clock control of glucose tolerance comes mainly from mouse models [<citation rid="B57-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/metabo14020126" pmid="38393018" pmcid="PMC10892663" count="1">57</citation>,<citation rid="B58-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2023.112588" pmid="37267101" pmcid="PMC10592114" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Whether meal, sleep or activity timing produces a distinct glucose-related phenotype in osteosarcopenia remains unknown; these variables should be recorded as potential modifiers.

Amino-acid and protein timing may link nutrition to both tissues. <sentence_start/>Muscle protein synthesis depends on amino-acid availability, mTORC1 signaling, insulin permissiveness and recent contractile activity, whereas bone matrix formation requires collagen substrates and an appropriate endocrine and energetic context. <sentence_start/>Branched-chain amino-acid catabolism is central to skeletal muscle and whole-body metabolism [<citation rid="B59-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2021.702826" pmid="34354601" pmcid="PMC8329528" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Total daily protein intake does not indicate how protein is distributed across meals or aligned with exercise, and whether such distribution alters bone-muscle outcomes in osteosarcopenia has not been directly tested.

Lipid and mitochondrial patterns provide a second bridge between metabolic disease and the proposed framework. <sentence_start/>Experimental circadian misalignment altered skeletal muscle lipid composition in healthy young men [<citation rid="B17-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202100143R" pmid="33977623" pmcid="PMC12315975" count="1">17</citation>], and age was associated with differences in the temporal plasma lipidome [<citation rid="B19-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s42003-023-05102-8" pmid="37474677" pmcid="PMC10359364" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Evidence that muscle clocks influence mitochondrial dynamics is largely mechanistic [<citation rid="B60-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1113/JP289019" pmid="40557866" count="1">60</citation>], and inactive-phase time-restricted feeding abolished daily variation in mitochondrial respiration in rat skeletal muscle [<citation rid="B55-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202100707R" pmid="35032416" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A single fasting sample cannot characterize diurnal variation, but the clinical value of repeated lipid or mitochondrial measurements in osteosarcopenia remains unestablished.

Redox, mineral-endocrine and microbial pathways extend the range of candidate mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Redox homeostasis is associated with skeletal muscle aging [<citation rid="B54-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox14091132" pmid="41009036" pmcid="PMC12466823" count="1">54</citation>], while glucocorticoid timing may influence muscle insulin sensitivity and skeletal remodeling [<citation rid="B11-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cmet.2026.05.002" pmid="42208534" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="B64-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1159/000512685" pmid="33130679" count="1">64</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Melatonin has been studied in relation to osteoblastogenesis, osteoclastogenesis and oxidative stress [<citation rid="B50-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphar.2022.866625" pmid="35645810" pmcid="PMC9130700" count="1">50</citation>,<citation rid="B65-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jpi.12814" pmid="35674448" count="1">65</citation>], and urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin rhythms were associated with a bone-resorption marker in blind women [<citation rid="B51-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jpi.70079" pmid="40960049" pmcid="PMC13048127" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Gut microbial metabolites may transmit feeding-time signals to immune and bone pathways [<citation rid="B52-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2025.1719445" pmid="42293411" pmcid="PMC13260651" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="B53-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.crmicr.2026.100561" pmid="41695578" pmcid="PMC12906124" count="1">53</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A recent cardiometabolic narrative review links gut-derived metabolites with mitochondrial redox dysfunction and ferroptosis but treats the complete pathway as hypothesis-generating; it therefore informs mechanism selection rather than osteosarcopenia-specific inference [<citation rid="B66-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/antiox15070803" pmid="42510534" pmcid="PMC13405568" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most evidence remains indirect or preclinical for osteosarcopenia; these axes are candidate or speculative mechanisms, not clinical biomarkers.
5. <sentence_start/>Temporal Bone-Muscle Crosstalk

The bone-muscle unit communicates through mechanical load, endocrine and paracrine factors, metabolites, extracellular vesicles, neural inputs, vascular supply and immune mediators. <sentence_start/>A temporal perspective raises four questions: when a signal is produced, when it is released, whether receptor sensitivity varies over time and whether target-tissue responses depend on biological or behavioral context. <sentence_start/>Table 3 summarizes the proposed routes and their evidentiary limits.

Mechanical loading is the most familiar bone-muscle signal. <sentence_start/>Exercise produces strain, myokine release, lactate flux, vascular shear, amino-acid demand and changes in insulin sensitivity. <sentence_start/>Bone responses to loading may differ with nutritional, endocrine and sleep context; time-of-day-dependent skeletal effects have so far been demonstrated mainly in mice [<citation rid="B49-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s42255-024-01057-0" pmid="38806654" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Direct clinical testing is required before extrapolating an optimal loading time to osteosarcopenia.

Secretory crosstalk may also be time-dependent. <sentence_start/>Myokines such as irisin, IL-6, IL-15, myostatin and IGF-1, and osteokines such as osteocalcin, sclerostin and FGF23, are influenced by activity, feeding, fasting, sleep and inflammation. <sentence_start/>The BMAL1/PGC1 4-FNDC5/irisin axis has been implicated in time-of-day resistance-exercise responses [<citation rid="B23-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jshs.2024.100968" pmid="39187065" pmcid="PMC11863284" count="1">23</citation>], while RANKL-related signaling is a plausible link between bone and muscle decline [<citation rid="B7-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1530/JOE-24-0093" pmid="38913537" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most human studies use one sampling time and cannot distinguish reduced production from altered timing.

Immune, vascular, endocrine and microbial routes broaden the model. <sentence_start/>Endothelial BMAL1 decline contributed to age-related bone loss in mice [<citation rid="B36-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI176660" pmid="39680455" pmcid="PMC11645155" count="1">36</citation>]; aging-related muscle <italic>Bmal1</italic> decline enhanced IL-1 -mediated osteoclastogenesis in a mouse model [<citation rid="B37-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/acel.70582" pmid="42259765" pmcid="PMC13246325" count="1">37</citation>]; and gut microbial metabolites have been implicated in experimental temporal regulation of bone homeostasis [<citation rid="B52-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fimmu.2025.1719445" pmid="42293411" pmcid="PMC13260651" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings generate mechanistic hypotheses but do not identify validated biomarkers or therapeutic targets in people with osteosarcopenia.
6. <sentence_start/>Chronometabolomics: Candidate Biomarkers and Study Designs

A standardized single measurement of glucose, C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), cortisol, amino acids or inflammatory markers may be clinically useful, but it cannot characterize within-day variation. <sentence_start/>Chronometabolomic research combines time-anchored or repeated metabolite sampling with information on sleep, light, meals, activity and medication. <sentence_start/>Repeated circulating measurements may estimate diurnal range, timing and robustness; demonstrating alignment between tissues requires tissue-specific measurements or validated proxies, and demonstrating endogenous circadian phase requires an appropriate marker or controlled protocol. <sentence_start/>Figure 4 and Table 4 summarize these distinctions.

A pragmatic design does not always require around-the-clock sampling. <sentence_start/>At minimum, investigators should standardize sampling time and report fasting duration, prior meal timing, sleep timing, recent activity and medication timing. <sentence_start/>Multiple daytime samples can characterize within-day variation, whereas dense 24-h sampling or a validated phase marker is required for robust circadian phase or amplitude estimation. <sentence_start/>Rest-activity studies in older women and men show that metabolites can track behavioral rhythm features [<citation rid="B20-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/sleep/zsaf320" pmid="41071097" pmcid="PMC12795739" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/sleep/zsaf319" pmid="41071109" pmcid="PMC12795748" count="1">21</citation>]; actigraphy can therefore contextualize metabolomics but should not be treated as a direct measure of endogenous phase.

Sleep duration, sleep quality and sleep disorders have been associated with sarcopenia or muscle loss [<citation rid="B43-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.maturitas.2025.108739" pmid="41016245" count="1">43</citation>,<citation rid="B67-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jamda.2023.04.032" pmid="37295459" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="B68-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11325-025-03519-5" pmid="41296131" count="1">68</citation>]; sleep quality, objective sleep parameters and sleep regularity have been associated with osteoporosis-related outcomes [<citation rid="B44-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jpi.70145" pmid="42126219" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B69-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.exger.2025.112844" pmid="40714125" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00198-026-08041-2" pmid="42056269" count="1">70</citation>]; and cortisol rhythm has been associated with sarcopenia in patients with type 2 diabetes [<citation rid="B71-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcsm.13727" pmid="39960018" pmcid="PMC11831345" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings are vulnerable to confounding, reverse causality and inconsistent timing metadata. <sentence_start/>They do not establish that sleep disruption causes osteosarcopenia or that rhythmic metabolites mediate the observed relationships. <sentence_start/>Complementary pathway-level blood metabolomics in cognitive aging associated lifestyle-related energy, amino-acid, lipid, inflammatory/redox and microbiome-linked patterns with grip strength, gait speed and frailty [<citation rid="B72-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-026-58782-7" pmid="42366201" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This supports integrating functional outcomes into metabolomic studies, but it neither evaluates temporal profiles nor validates biomarkers in osteosarcopenia. <sentence_start/>Future studies should pair clinical phenotyping with repeated metabolite sampling, objective sleep/activity data and medication and nutrition records.
7. Candidate Time-Targeted Interventions: Research Rationale and Safety

None of the timing strategies discussed in this section has been validated as an osteosarcopenia-specific treatment. <sentence_start/>Their inclusion does not constitute clinical advice or support a universal optimal treatment time. <sentence_start/>Older adults differ by chronotype, frailty, medication schedule, comorbidities, appetite, fall risk, caregiving environment and social constraints. <sentence_start/>Light, diet, exercise and medication timing can be evaluated as coordinated research exposures [<citation rid="B73-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2025.1698016" pmid="41404509" pmcid="PMC12702709" count="1">73</citation>], but established osteoporosis and sarcopenia care should not be delayed or replaced. <sentence_start/>Table 5 summarizes the evidence status, clinical readiness and principal safeguards.

Chrononutrition requires particular caution. <sentence_start/>Energy-intake timing is being discussed as a candidate modifier of aging biology [<citation rid="B74-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/gerona/glad069" pmid="37325958" pmcid="PMC10272989" count="1">74</citation>], and a short-term crossover trial in adults with type 2 diabetes reported improved glucose homeostasis, but not improved insulin sensitivity, during time-restricted eating [<citation rid="B47-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00125-022-05752-z" pmid="35871650" pmcid="PMC9477920" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Bone-focused evidence remains mixed, and changes accompanying weight loss complicate interpretation [<citation rid="B48-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu16060876" pmid="38542787" pmcid="PMC10974430" count="1">48</citation>,<citation rid="B75-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/oby.23577" pmid="36239695" pmcid="PMC10092311" count="1">75</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Any osteosarcopenia trial should prespecify safeguards against inadequate energy, protein, calcium and micronutrient intake and should exclude or closely supervise participants with frailty, low body mass index, malnutrition risk, kidney disease or glucose-lowering medication. <sentence_start/>Protein distribution, meal quality and coordination with exercise are higher-priority trial questions than fasting duration alone.

Exercise timing is also investigational. <sentence_start/>Human evidence comes largely from type 2 diabetes or other populations without defined osteosarcopenia, while several mechanistic findings derive from experimental models [<citation rid="B22-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.metabol.2022.155268" pmid="35908579" count="1">22</citation>,<citation rid="B23-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jshs.2024.100968" pmid="39187065" pmcid="PMC11863284" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="B24-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202402930R" pmid="39902884" pmcid="PMC11792768" count="1">24</citation>,<citation rid="B25-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2504080122" pmid="40627397" pmcid="PMC12280960" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B76-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13105-024-01066-3" pmid="39715985" count="1">76</citation>,<citation rid="B77-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/10715762.2024.2348789" pmid="38946540" count="1">77</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Reviews discuss exercise as a potential timing cue for peripheral clocks [<citation rid="B78-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/07420528.2022.2050384" pmid="35282722" count="1">78</citation>,<citation rid="B79-metabolites-16-00547" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph182412949" pmid="34948558" pmcid="PMC8702158" count="1">79</citation>], but the safest feasible time should be individualized around chronotype, cardiovascular status, fatigue, sleep and fall risk. <sentence_start/>Exercise itself remains central to muscle, balance and bone health; current data justify osteosarcopenia-specific timing trials, not a single recommended exercise hour.

Medication schedules should not be changed by patients on the basis of this framework. <sentence_start/>Timing studies must be indication-specific and clinician-led, account for kidney function, diabetes treatment, glucocorticoid exposure and polypharmacy, and distinguish pharmacokinetic convenience from improved bone-muscle outcomes.
Figure 5 summarizes this proposed, investigational workflow.
8. <sentence_start/>Discussion
8.1. <sentence_start/>Interpretation of the Evidence

The principal finding of this review is a mismatch between biological plausibility and disease-specific evidence. <sentence_start/>Human studies demonstrate time-of-day variation in bone turnover markers and skeletal muscle metabolism and show associations between behavioral rhythms and bone or muscle outcomes. <sentence_start/>Experimental models identify plausible clock-dependent pathways. <sentence_start/>However, no identified human study combined a defined osteosarcopenia phenotype, a validated endogenous phase marker and serial metabolomic profiling. <sentence_start/>The proposed framework is therefore integrative and hypothesis-generating; it does not establish a distinct causal subtype of osteosarcopenia.

Several uncertainties limit synthesis. <sentence_start/>Circadian, diurnal and rest-activity measures are not interchangeable. <sentence_start/>Metabolite timing depends on chronotype, light, meals, acute exercise, posture, sleep, medication and comorbidity, while cross-sectional associations cannot distinguish cause from consequence. <sentence_start/>Evidence on time-restricted eating and skeletal outcomes is mixed and may be confounded by weight loss or reduced nutrient intake. <sentence_start/>Exercise studies differ in population, mode, intensity and timing reference, and they do not support a universal optimal time. <sentence_start/>Tissue-specific clock-gene models establish mechanistic possibilities but may not reproduce multimorbidity, frailty or polypharmacy in older adults.
8.2. <sentence_start/>Incremental Clinical Value and Feasibility

Chronometabolomics must demonstrate value beyond existing assessment. <sentence_start/>DXA, fracture history and risk tools, grip strength, chair-rise and gait-speed tests, lean-mass measures, routine laboratory tests and standardized bone-turnover markers already support diagnosis and risk stratification. <sentence_start/>Rhythm-derived variables would be clinically useful only if they improve diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection or longitudinal monitoring beyond these tools with acceptable cost and participant burden. <sentence_start/>At present, chronometabolomics should neither replace established diagnostic criteria nor delay evidence-based osteoporosis, nutrition, exercise or fall-prevention care.

Repeated sampling introduces participant burden, possible sleep disturbance, incomplete adherence, assay batch effects, cost and unstable phase estimates from sparse observations. <sentence_start/>A staged strategy may be more feasible: standardized single-time sampling for routine comparability; several targeted daytime samples for within-day variation; and dense 24-h sampling or validated phase markers for mechanistic circadian studies. <sentence_start/>Home or minimally invasive sampling may reduce burden but requires analytical validation. <sentence_start/>Protocols should prespecify temporal endpoints and distinguish clock time, biological phase and behavior.
8.3. Research Priorities

Direct cohorts should include healthy controls, isolated osteoporosis or osteopenia, isolated sarcopenia and combined osteosarcopenia. <sentence_start/>Participants should be characterized by sex, menopausal status, diabetes, kidney function, glucocorticoid exposure, medications, chronotype, sleep disorders, physical activity and nutrition. <sentence_start/>Timing metadata should be treated as primary data, and candidate signatures should be externally validated against clinically meaningful outcomes.

Triangulation across tissue-specific models, longitudinal cohorts, randomized trials and Mendelian-randomization analyses may strengthen causal inference, although each design has distinct assumptions and limitations. <sentence_start/>Trials should test whether time-targeted strategies add benefit beyond adequate protein and calcium intake, resistance and balance exercise, fall prevention and standard pharmacological care. <sentence_start/>Feasibility, safety, adherence, quality of life, falls and fractures should accompany metabolomic and rhythm endpoints.
9. Limitations of This Review

This review has several limitations. <sentence_start/>It is a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review; no prospective protocol, exhaustive record-level screening log, quantitative synthesis, formal risk-of-bias assessment or certainty-of-evidence evaluation was undertaken. <sentence_start/>Purposive selection of representative studies may have introduced selection and citation bias. <sentence_start/>Definitions of osteosarcopenia, sarcopenia and osteoporosis, as well as populations, sampling schedules, analytical platforms and outcomes, were heterogeneous. <sentence_start/>Much of the evidence was extrapolated from component disorders, metabolically compromised populations or experimental models, and most proposed biomarkers and interventions lack osteosarcopenia-specific validation. <sentence_start/>The search emphasized English-language bibliographic interfaces and may not have captured all regional or non-indexed literature. <sentence_start/>The rapidly evolving literature may also alter the balance of evidence. <sentence_start/>These limitations preclude causal inference, definition of diagnostic thresholds or recommendation of optimal intervention times.
10. Conclusions

Chronometabolomics is a promising research framework for testing whether temporal metabolic disorganization contributes to coupled bone and muscle decline. <sentence_start/>Current evidence is dominated by component-specific human studies and mechanistic or preclinical models; direct osteosarcopenia studies with repeated temporal profiling remain insufficient to establish diagnostic biomarkers, causal pathways or optimal treatment timing. <sentence_start/>Future studies should combine consensus bone-muscle phenotyping, standardized timing metadata, repeated or targeted sampling and safety-focused prospective trials, and should test whether rhythm-derived measures add value beyond existing clinical tools. <sentence_start/>Until such evidence is available, time-targeted interventions should remain individualized research candidates rather than routine recommendations for osteosarcopenia.
